title: Der Stiefel von Büffelleder
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 199. Text from Wikisource („Der Stiefel von Büffelleder (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: KHM 199 opens with a maxim — a soldier who fears nothing troubles himself about nothing — and then shows one: discharged and begging his way in an old weather-cloak and a pair of buffalo-leather riding boots, he falls in with a well-dressed huntsman lost in the same forest and cheerfully calls him Bruder Wichsstiefel, brother polished-boots. The old woman who opens the door of the house they find that night tells them it is a robbers’ den; the soldier walks in anyway, eats at the robbers’ table, has their best wine fetched up, and with a toast — mouths open, right hands in the air — leaves all twelve sitting motionless as stone until he has brought his old comrades out from the town to bind them. Only then does the huntsman open his coat on royal clothes: the king says the soldier has saved his life and will never want again, on the one condition that he ask permission before proposing any more healths.

sentences.t: Ein Soldat, der sich vor nichts fürchtet, kümmert sich auch um nichts.
sentences.l: A soldier who fears nothing troubles himself about nothing either.
sentences.i: A soldier who is afraid of nothing does not trouble himself about anything either.
sentences.n: “sich fürchten vor” and “sich kümmern um” are both reflexive and both fix their preposition; German states the general case in the present tense, as a maxim.

sentences.t: So einer hatte seinen Abschied erhalten, und da er nichts gelernt hatte und nichts verdienen konnte, so zog er umher und bat gute Leute um ein Almosen.
sentences.l: Such a one had received his discharge, and since he had learnt nothing and could earn nothing, so he went about and asked good people for an alms.
sentences.i: Such a one had got his discharge, and since he had learnt no trade and could earn nothing, he went wandering about and begged an alms of kindly people.
sentences.n: “Abschied erhalten” is the fixed phrase for being let out of the army. “jemanden um etwas bitten” takes the person in the accusative and the thing after “um”.

sentences.t: Auf seinen Schultern hieng ein alter Wettermantel, und ein paar Reiterstiefeln von Büffelleder waren ihm auch noch geblieben.
sentences.l: On his shoulders hung an old weather-cloak, and a pair of riding-boots of buffalo-leather had also still been left to him.
sentences.i: An old weather-cloak hung on his shoulders, and a pair of riding-boots of buffalo leather were all that was left to him besides.
sentences.n: “hieng” is the 1857 spelling of hing. The boots arrive in the second sentence of the tale and give it its title; nothing yet says why they matter.

sentences.t: Eines Tages gieng er, ohne auf Weg und Steg zu achten, immer ins Feld hinein und gelangte endlich in einen Wald.
sentences.l: One day he went, without heeding path or track, ever on into the open country and came at last into a forest.
sentences.i: One day, taking no heed of path or track, he walked on and on into open country and came at last to a forest.
sentences.n: “eines Tages” is a genitive of time. “Weg und Steg” is a set pair — road and footbridge — for any way at all.

sentences.t: Er wußte nicht wo er war, sah aber auf einem abgehauenen Baumstamm einen Mann sitzen, der gut gekleidet war und einen grünen Jägerrock trug.
sentences.l: He did not know where he was, but saw on a hewn-down tree-trunk a man sitting who was well dressed and wore a green huntsman’s coat.
sentences.i: He did not know where he was, but he saw a man sitting on a felled tree-trunk, well dressed and wearing a green huntsman’s coat.
sentences.n: “sah … einen Mann sitzen” — German reports perception with a bare infinitive where English needs a participle. The green coat is the whole disguise: a Jägerrock is what a huntsman wears, and the soldier takes the wearer for one.

sentences.t: Der Soldat reichte ihm die Hand, ließ sich neben ihm auf das Gras nieder und streckte seine Beine aus.
sentences.l: The soldier reached him the hand, let himself down beside him on the grass and stretched his legs out.
sentences.i: The soldier gave him his hand, settled down beside him on the grass and stretched out his legs.
sentences.n: “sich niederlassen” is separable and reflexive: to let oneself down, to settle. “ausstrecken” likewise puts its particle at the end.

sentences.t: „Ich sehe du hast feine Stiefel an, die glänzend gewichst sind“ sagte er zu dem Jäger, „wenn du aber herum ziehen müßtest wie ich, so würden sie nicht lange halten.
sentences.l: “I see you have fine boots on, that are polished till they shine,” he said to the huntsman, “but if you had to wander about like me, then they would not last long.
sentences.i: “I see you have fine boots on, polished till they shine,” he said to the huntsman, “but if you had to tramp about as I do, they would not last long.
sentences.n: The soldier speaks to a stranger with “du”, the familiar form, which is exactly what he will apologise for at the end. “gewichst” is from Wichse, boot-blacking.

sentences.t: Schau die meinigen an, die sind von Büffelleder und haben schon lange gedient, gehen aber durch dick und dünn.“
sentences.l: Look at mine, they are of buffalo-leather and have served long already, but go through thick and thin.”
sentences.i: Look at mine: they are of buffalo leather and have been in service a long while, but they go through thick and thin.”
sentences.n: “schau … an” is anschauen, to look at, with the particle at the end. German has the same “durch dick und dünn” as English, and it is as old in both.

sentences.t: Nach einer Weile stand der Soldat auf und sprach „ich kann nicht länger bleiben, der Hunger treibt mich fort.
sentences.l: After a while the soldier stood up and said “I cannot stay longer, hunger drives me away.
sentences.i: After a while the soldier got up and said, “I can stay no longer; hunger is driving me on.
sentences.n: “aufstehen” is separable, “stand … auf”. “fort” at the end is the particle of forttreiben, to drive away.

sentences.t: Aber, Bruder Wichsstiefel, wohinaus geht der Weg?“
sentences.l: But, brother Polished-boots, which way out goes the road?”
sentences.i: But, brother Polished-boots, which way does the road go?”
sentences.n: “Wichsstiefel” — a boot kept blacked and shining, said of the man wearing them; the soldier is teasing a stranger he takes for an equal. “wohinaus” asks which way out.

sentences.t: „Ich weiß es selber nicht“ antwortete der Jäger, „ich habe mich in dem Wald verirrt.“
sentences.l: “I do not know it myself,” answered the huntsman, “I have lost my way in the forest.”
sentences.i: “I do not know myself,” answered the huntsman, “I have lost my way in the forest.”
sentences.n: “weiß” here is the verb wissen, to know, spelled like the adjective “white”. “sich verirren” is reflexive: to go astray.

sentences.t: „So geht dirs ja, wie mir“ sprach der Soldat, „gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern, wir wollen bei einander bleiben und den Weg suchen.“
sentences.l: “Then it goes for you just as for me,” said the soldier, “like and like keep company gladly, we will stay together and look for the way.”
sentences.i: “Then you are in the same case as I am,” said the soldier. “Like keeps company with like — we will stay together and look for the way.”
sentences.n: “dirs” is “dir es” run together. “gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern” is a proverb, and the reflexive “sich gesellen” means to join company.

sentences.t: Der Jäger lächelte ein wenig, und sie giengen zusammen fort immer weiter, bis die Nacht einbrach.
sentences.l: The huntsman smiled a little, and they went on together ever further, until the night fell.
sentences.i: The huntsman smiled a little, and they went on together, further and further, until night fell.
sentences.n: The smile is the only sign the printing gives that the huntsman knows something the soldier does not; it is left entirely to the reader. “einbrechen”, of night, is to close in.

sentences.t: „Wir kommen aus dem Wald nicht heraus“ sprach der Soldat, „aber ich sehe dort in der Ferne ein Licht schimmern, da wirds etwas zu essen geben.“
sentences.l: “We are not getting out of the forest,” said the soldier, “but I see a light shimmering there in the distance, there will be something to eat there.”
sentences.i: “We shall never get out of this forest,” said the soldier, “but I see a light glimmering in the distance — there will be something to eat there.”
sentences.n: “wirds” is “wird es”. “es wird geben” is the German for “there will be”.

sentences.t: Sie fanden ein Steinhaus, klopften an die Thüre und ein altes Weib öffnete.
sentences.l: They found a stone house, knocked at the door and an old woman opened.
sentences.i: They found a stone house, knocked at the door, and an old woman opened it.
sentences.n: “Thüre” is the 1857 spelling of Türe. German leaves “öffnete” without an object where English wants “opened it”.

sentences.t: „Wir suchen ein Nachtquartier“ sprach der Soldat, „und etwas Unterfutter für den Magen, denn der meinige ist so leer wie ein alter Tornister.“
sentences.l: “We are looking for a night’s quarters,” said the soldier, “and a bit of lining for the stomach, for mine is as empty as an old knapsack.”
sentences.i: “We are looking for a night’s lodging,” said the soldier, “and a little lining for the stomach, for mine is as empty as an old knapsack.”
sentences.n: “Unterfutter” is the lining sewn inside a coat; the soldier’s joke is to ask for some for his stomach. A Tornister is the pack a soldier carries on his back.

sentences.t: „Hier könnt ihr nicht bleiben,“ antwortete die Alte, „das ist ein Räuberhaus,
sentences.l: “Here you cannot stay,” answered the old woman, “this is a robbers’ house,
sentences.i: “You cannot stay here,” answered the old woman, “this is a robbers’ house,
sentences.n: “die Alte” is the adjective alt used as a noun for a woman — the old one. She is the household’s servant, and the tale never says more about her.

sentences.t: und ihr thut am klügsten daß ihr euch fortmacht, bevor sie heim kommen, denn finden sie euch, so seid ihr verloren.“
sentences.l: and you do most cleverly if you take yourselves off before they come home, for if they find you, then you are lost.”
sentences.i: and you would do best to be off before they come home, for if they find you, you are lost.”
sentences.n: “am klügsten thun” — to act most wisely; “thut” is the 1857 spelling of tut. “finden sie euch” is a conditional with the verb first and no “wenn”.

sentences.t: „Es wird so schlimm nicht sein,“ antwortete der Soldat, „ich habe seit zwei Tagen keinen Bissen genossen, und es ist mir einerlei ob ich hier umkomme oder im Wald vor Hunger sterbe.
sentences.l: “It will not be so bad,” answered the soldier, “I have not had a bite for two days, and it is all one to me whether I perish here or die of hunger in the forest.
sentences.i: “It will not be as bad as that,” answered the soldier. “I have not had a bite for two days, and it is all one to me whether I come to grief here or starve to death in the forest.
sentences.n: “seit zwei Tagen” with a present-perfect verb is German’s way of measuring a stretch running up to now. “einerlei” — all one, all the same, and the person stands in the dative.

sentences.t: Ich gehe herein.“
sentences.l: I am going in.”
sentences.n: “herein” is inward and toward the person spoken to — the door is in front of him as he says it.

sentences.t: Der Jäger wollte nicht folgen, aber der Soldat zog ihn am Ermel mit sich: „komm, Bruderherz, es wird nicht gleich an den Kragen gehen.“
sentences.l: The huntsman did not want to follow, but the soldier pulled him by the sleeve with him: “come, brother-heart, it will not go straight at our collars.”
sentences.i: The huntsman would not follow, but the soldier drew him along by the sleeve. “Come, brother-heart, it will not cost us our necks at once.”
sentences.n: “Ermel” is the 1857 spelling of Ärmel. “einem an den Kragen gehen” — to go for someone’s collar — means to put a life in danger; “Bruderherz” is coaxing, halfway between brother and old fellow.

sentences.t: Die Alte hatte Mitleiden und sagte „kriecht hinter den Ofen, wenn sie etwas übrig lassen und eingeschlafen sind, so will ichs euch zustecken.“
sentences.l: The old woman had compassion and said “crawl behind the stove, when they leave something over and have fallen asleep, then I will slip it to you.”
sentences.i: The old woman took pity and said, “creep behind the stove; when they have left something over and fallen asleep, I will slip it to you.”
sentences.n: “kriecht” is an order here, the plural imperative of kriechen. “zustecken” is to pass something to someone on the quiet.

sentences.t: Kaum saßen sie in der Ecke, so kamen zwölf Räuber herein gestürmt, setzten sich an den Tisch, der schon gedeckt war, und forderten mit Ungestüm das Essen.
sentences.l: Hardly were they sitting in the corner, when twelve robbers came storming in, set themselves at the table, which was already laid, and demanded the food with vehemence.
sentences.i: They had hardly settled in the corner when twelve robbers came storming in, sat down at the table, which was already laid, and noisily demanded their food.
sentences.n: “kaum … so” works like English “no sooner … than”, with the inversion obligatory in German. “mit Ungestüm” — with impetuousness, boisterously.

sentences.t: Die Alte trug einen großen Braten herein, und die Räuber ließen sichs wohl schmecken.
sentences.l: The old woman carried a great roast in, and the robbers let it taste them well.
sentences.i: The old woman carried in a great roast, and the robbers fell to with relish.
sentences.n: “sich etwas schmecken lassen” is to let a thing taste good to one — to eat with enjoyment; “sichs” is “sich es” run together.

sentences.t: Als der Geruch von der Speise dem Soldaten in die Nase stieg, sagte er zum Jäger „ich halts nicht länger aus, ich setze mich an den Tisch und esse mit.“
sentences.l: When the smell of the food rose to the soldier in the nose, he said to the huntsman “I cannot hold out any longer, I am sitting myself at the table and eating with them.”
sentences.i: When the smell of the food reached the soldier’s nose, he said to the huntsman, “I cannot hold out any longer; I am going to sit down at the table and eat with them.”
sentences.n: “dem Soldaten in die Nase” uses the dative for the person whose nose it is. “halts” is “halte es”, and “aushalten” is separable: halt … aus.

sentences.t: „Du bringst uns ums Leben“ sprach der Jäger und hielt ihn am Arm.
sentences.l: “You are bringing us out of life,” said the huntsman and held him by the arm.
sentences.i: “You will be the death of us,” said the huntsman, holding him by the arm.
sentences.n: “ums Leben bringen” — to bring someone out of their life, the German for killing them; “ums” is “um das”.

sentences.t: Aber der Soldat fieng an laut zu husten.
sentences.l: But the soldier began to cough loudly.
sentences.n: “fieng … an” is anfangen with the particle at the end; the 1857 spelling of fing.

sentences.t: Als die Räuber das hörten, warfen sie Messer und Gabel hin, sprangen auf und entdeckten die beiden hinter dem Ofen.
sentences.l: When the robbers heard that, they threw knife and fork down, sprang up and discovered the two behind the stove.
sentences.i: When the robbers heard it, they threw down knife and fork, sprang up, and discovered the pair behind the stove.
sentences.n: German counts “Messer und Gabel” in the singular where English can too, and “hin” is the particle of hinwerfen, to throw down.

sentences.t: „Aha, ihr Herrn,“ riefen sie, „sitzt ihr in der Ecke?
sentences.l: “Aha, gentlemen,” they cried, “are you sitting in the corner?
sentences.i: “Aha, my fine gentlemen,” they cried, “so you are sitting in the corner?
sentences.n: “Herrn” is the shortened plural of Herr; the robbers are being sarcastic with a form of address they do not mean.

sentences.t: was wollt ihr hier? seid ihr als Kundschafter ausgeschickt?
sentences.l: what do you want here? are you sent out as spies?
sentences.i: what do you want here? have you been sent out to spy?
sentences.n: “ausgeschickt” is the past participle of ausschicken, separable. “Kundschafter” is the same in singular and plural.

sentences.t: wartet, ihr sollt an einem dürren Ast das Fliegen lernen.“
sentences.l: wait, you shall learn flying on a withered branch.”
sentences.i: wait — you shall learn to fly from a dry branch.”
sentences.n: The threat is hanging, said in the tale’s own dry manner: the flying is what a body does at the end of a rope. “das Fliegen” is the infinitive used as a noun.

sentences.t: „Nur manierlich“ sprach der Soldat, „mich hungert, gebt mir zu essen, hernach könnt ihr mit mir machen was ihr wollt.“
sentences.l: “Only mannerly,” said the soldier, “I am hungry, give me to eat, afterwards you can do with me what you want.”
sentences.i: “Mind your manners,” said the soldier. “I am hungry — give me something to eat, and afterwards you can do what you like with me.”
sentences.n: “mich hungert” is impersonal, with the hungry person in the accusative; modern German says “ich bin hungrig”. “hernach” is the older “afterwards”.

sentences.t: Die Räuber stutzten und der Anführer sprach „ich sehe du fürchtest dich nicht, gut, Essen sollst du haben, aber hernach mußt du sterben.“
sentences.l: The robbers were taken aback and the leader said “I see you are not afraid, good, food you shall have, but afterwards you must die.”
sentences.i: The robbers were taken aback, and the leader said, “I see you are not afraid. Good — you shall have food, but afterwards you must die.”
sentences.n: “stutzen” is to stop short in surprise. “Essen sollst du haben” puts the object first for emphasis, which German can do and English cannot.

sentences.t: „Das wird sich finden“ sagte der Soldat, setzte sich an den Tisch und fieng an tapfer in den Braten einzuhauen.
sentences.l: “That will find itself,” said the soldier, sat himself at the table and began to hew bravely into the roast.
sentences.i: “That remains to be seen,” said the soldier; he sat down at the table and began laying into the roast.
sentences.n: “das wird sich finden” is a set phrase — we shall see. “einhauen” is to strike into something; “einzuhauen” puts the “zu” inside the separable verb.

sentences.t: „Bruder Wichsstiefel, komm und iß,“ rief er dem Jäger zu, „du wirst hungrig sein, so gut als ich, und einen bessern Braten kannst du zu Haus nicht haben;“ aber der Jäger wollte nicht essen.
sentences.l: “Brother Polished-boots, come and eat,” he called to the huntsman, “you will be hungry, just as much as I, and a better roast you cannot have at home;” but the huntsman did not want to eat.
sentences.i: “Brother Polished-boots, come and eat,” he called across to the huntsman, “you must be as hungry as I am, and you will get no better roast at home;” but the huntsman would not eat.
sentences.n: “so gut als ich” — the 1857 text uses “als” in comparisons where modern German uses “wie”. The soldier is telling a king he could not eat better at home, which is the joke the reader is given and the soldier is not.

sentences.t: Die Räuber sahen dem Soldaten mit Erstaunen zu und sagten „der Kerl macht keine Umstände.“
sentences.l: The robbers watched the soldier with astonishment and said “the fellow makes no fuss.”
sentences.i: The robbers watched the soldier in astonishment and said, “the fellow makes no bones about it.”
sentences.n: “zusehen” takes the dative of the person watched. “keine Umstände machen” is to make no ceremony, no fuss.

sentences.t: Hernach sprach er „das Essen wäre schon gut, nun schafft auch einen guten Trunk herbei.“
sentences.l: Afterwards he said “the food would be good enough, now bring a good drink here as well.”
sentences.i: Afterwards he said, “the food is well enough — now bring up a good drink too.”
sentences.n: “wäre” is a polite, off-hand subjunctive: it would be good, as it were. “herbeischaffen” is separable, and the particle stands at the end.

sentences.t: Der Anführer war in der Laune sich das auch noch gefallen zu lassen und rief der Alten zu „hol eine Flasche aus dem Keller und zwar von dem besten.“
sentences.l: The leader was in the humour to put up with that too and called to the old woman “fetch a bottle out of the cellar, and that of the best.”
sentences.i: The leader was in the humour to allow him that too, and called to the old woman, “fetch a bottle from the cellar, and let it be of the best.”
sentences.n: “sich etwas gefallen lassen” is to let a thing be done to one, to put up with it. “und zwar” singles out what has just been said: and that, specifically.

sentences.t: Der Soldat zog den Pfropfen heraus daß es knallte,
sentences.l: The soldier drew the cork out so that it banged,
sentences.i: The soldier drew the cork with a pop,
sentences.n: “daß es knallte” — a result clause: so that there was a bang.

sentences.t: gieng mit der Flasche zu dem Jäger und sprach „gib acht, Bruder, du sollst dein blaues Wunder sehen:
sentences.l: went with the bottle to the huntsman and said “take heed, brother, you shall see your blue wonder:
sentences.i: went over to the huntsman with the bottle and said, “pay attention, brother, you are in for a surprise:
sentences.n: “sein blaues Wunder sehen” — to see one’s blue wonder — is to get an astonishment, usually an unpleasant one; the colour has no meaning left in it.

sentences.t: jetzt will ich eine Gesundheit auf die ganze Sippschaft ausbringen.“
sentences.l: now I will bring out a health upon the whole clan.”
sentences.i: now I will drink a health to the whole crew.”
sentences.n: “eine Gesundheit ausbringen” is to propose a toast. “Sippschaft” is a clan or tribe, said with contempt — this lot, the whole crew of them.

sentences.t: Dann schwenkte er die Flasche über den Köpfen der Räuber, rief „ihr sollt alle leben, aber das Maul auf und die rechte Hand in der Höhe“ und that einen herzhaften Zug.
sentences.l: Then he swung the bottle over the heads of the robbers, called “you shall all live, but the mouth open and the right hand up in the air,” and took a hearty draught.
sentences.i: Then he swung the bottle over the robbers’ heads and cried, “long life to you all — but mouths open and right hands in the air!” and took a hearty pull at it.
sentences.n: “ihr sollt alle leben” is word for word “you shall all live”, and it is the ordinary German toast; here it turns out to be the spell. The order that follows has no verb at all — the naming of mouth and hand is the whole command.

sentences.t: Kaum waren die Worte heraus, so saßen sie alle bewegungslos als wären sie von Stein, hatten das Maul offen und streckten den rechten Arm in die Höhe.
sentences.l: Hardly were the words out, when they all sat motionless as if they were of stone, had their mouths open and stretched the right arm up in the air.
sentences.i: The words were hardly out before they all sat motionless, as though they were made of stone, their mouths open and their right arms held up in the air.
sentences.n: “als wären sie” is the subjunctive of comparison, with the verb first and no “wenn”. “Maul” is the mouth of an animal, and using it of people is contemptuous.

sentences.t: Der Jäger sprach zu dem Soldaten „ich sehe du kannst noch andere Kunststücke, aber nun komm und laß uns heim gehen.“
sentences.l: The huntsman said to the soldier “I see you can do still other tricks, but now come and let us go home.”
sentences.i: The huntsman said to the soldier, “I see you know other tricks as well; but now come, and let us go home.”
sentences.n: “du kannst noch andere Kunststücke” has no second verb: können on its own can mean to know how to do a thing.

sentences.t: „Oho, Bruderherz, das wäre zu früh abmarschiert, wir haben den Feind geschlagen und wollen erst Beute machen.
sentences.l: “Oho, brother-heart, that would be marched off too early, we have beaten the enemy and want first to make booty.
sentences.i: “Oho, brother-heart, that would be striking camp too soon; we have beaten the enemy, and now we will take our spoils.
sentences.n: The soldier keeps to army language throughout — marching off, the beaten enemy, booty. “abmarschiert” has no subject in the German either.

sentences.t: Die sitzen da fest und sperren das Maul vor Verwunderung auf: sie dürfen sich aber nicht rühren bis ich es erlaube.
sentences.l: Those sit there fast and gape their mouths open with astonishment: they may not however stir until I allow it.
sentences.i: There they sit fast, gaping with astonishment; but they cannot stir until I give them leave.
sentences.n: “die” at the head of the sentence is a demonstrative used for people, blunter than “sie”. “sperren … auf” is aufsperren, to open wide.

sentences.t: Komm iß und trink.“
sentences.l: Come, eat and drink.”
sentences.n: Three bare imperatives; “iß” is the 1857 spelling of iss.

sentences.t: Die Alte mußte noch eine Flasche von dem besten holen, und der Soldat stand nicht eher auf als bis er wieder für drei Tage gegessen hatte.
sentences.l: The old woman had to fetch another bottle of the best, and the soldier did not stand up sooner than until he had eaten again for three days.
sentences.i: The old woman had to fetch another bottle of the best, and the soldier did not get up until he had eaten enough for three days over again.
sentences.n: “nicht eher … als bis” is the German frame for “not until”, and it takes both halves to build it.

sentences.t: Endlich als der Tag kam, sagte er „nun ist Zeit daß wir das Zelt abbrechen, und damit wir einen kurzen Marsch haben, so soll die Alte uns den nächsten Weg nach der Stadt zeigen.“
sentences.l: At last, when the day came, he said “now it is time that we break up the tent, and so that we have a short march, the old woman shall show us the nearest way to the town.”
sentences.i: At last, when day came, he said, “now it is time to strike camp, and so that we have a short march of it, the old woman shall show us the nearest way to the town.”
sentences.n: “das Zelt abbrechen” is to strike a tent — army speech again, for two men who have slept behind a stove. “damit” introduces a purpose.

sentences.t: Als sie dort angelangt waren, gieng er zu seinen alten Kameraden und sprach „ich habe draußen im Wald ein Nest voll Galgenvögel aufgefunden, kommt mit, wir wollen es ausheben.“
sentences.l: When they had arrived there, he went to his old comrades and said “I have found out in the forest a nest full of gallows-birds, come along, we will clear it out.”
sentences.i: When they had got there he went to his old comrades and said, “out in the forest I have found a nest full of gallows-birds; come along, and we will clear it out.”
sentences.n: “Galgenvögel” — gallows-birds — is an old name for rogues fit for hanging, and it sets up the bird-catching picture that follows. “ausheben” is used both of robbing a nest and of rounding up a band.

sentences.t: Der Soldat führte sie an und sprach zu dem Jäger „du mußt wieder mit zurück und zusehen wie sie flattern, wenn wir sie an den Füßen packen.“
sentences.l: The soldier led them on and said to the huntsman “you must come back along too and watch how they flutter when we grab them by the feet.”
sentences.i: The soldier led them out and said to the huntsman, “you must come back with us too, and see how they flutter when we take them by the feet.”
sentences.n: “anführen” is separable, to lead a body of men. The nest, the fluttering and the feet keep the same picture running for three sentences.

sentences.t: Er stellte die Mannschaft rings um die Räuber herum, dann nahm er die Flasche, trank einen Schluck, schwenkte sie über ihnen her und rief „ihr sollt alle leben!“
sentences.l: He placed the men round about the robbers, then took he the bottle, drank a mouthful, swung it over them and called “you shall all live!”
sentences.i: He posted his men all round the robbers, then took the bottle, drank a mouthful, swung it over them and cried, “long life to you all!”
sentences.n: The words that laid the spell lift it again; nothing else is needed, and the tale explains nothing. “rings … herum” is all the way round, and the “her” in “über ihnen her” carries the sweep of the bottle across them.

sentences.t: Augenblicklich hatten sie ihre Bewegung wieder, wurden aber niedergeworfen und an Händen und Füßen mit Stricken gebunden.
sentences.l: Instantly they had their movement again, but were thrown down and bound at hands and feet with ropes.
sentences.i: In an instant they had the use of their limbs again, but they were thrown down and bound hand and foot with ropes.
sentences.n: “Stricken” here is the dative plural of der Strick, a rope, not the verb stricken, to knit. “niedergeworfen” is separable nieder-.

sentences.t: Dann hieß sie der Soldat wie Säcke auf einen Wagen werfen und sagte „fahrt sie nur gleich vor das Gefängnis.“
sentences.l: Then the soldier bade them be thrown like sacks onto a cart and said “just drive them straight in front of the prison.”
sentences.i: Then the soldier had them thrown like sacks onto a cart and said, “drive them straight to the prison.”
sentences.n: “heißen” with a bare infinitive means to order someone to do something — “hieß … werfen”, bade them throw. “fahrt” is the plural imperative of fahren.

sentences.t: Der Jäger aber nahm einen von der Mannschaft bei Seite und gab ihm noch eine Bestellung mit.
sentences.l: The huntsman however took one of the men aside and gave him yet an errand along with him.
sentences.i: But the huntsman took one of the men aside and gave him an errand to carry besides.
sentences.n: “mitgeben” is separable — to give something to someone to take with them; the errand’s content is kept from the reader as carefully as the huntsman’s name.

sentences.t: „Bruder Wichsstiefel,“ sprach der Soldat, „wir haben den Feind glücklich überrumpelt und uns wohl genährt, jetzt wollen wir als Nachzügler in aller Ruhe hinter her marschieren.“
sentences.l: “Brother Polished-boots,” said the soldier, “we have luckily taken the enemy by surprise and fed ourselves well, now we will march along behind as stragglers, at our ease.”
sentences.i: “Brother Polished-boots,” said the soldier, “we have taken the enemy nicely by surprise and fed ourselves well; now we will bring up the rear like stragglers, at our ease.”
sentences.n: “glücklich” in the older sense is successfully rather than happily. A Nachzügler is the man who lags behind a marching column.

sentences.t: Als sie sich der Stadt näherten, so sah der Soldat wie sich eine Menge Menschen aus dem Stadtthor drängten, lautes Freudengeschrei erhuben und grüne Zweige in der Luft schwangen.
sentences.l: When they drew near to the town, the soldier saw how a crowd of people pressed out of the town gate, raised loud shouts of joy and swung green branches in the air.
sentences.i: As they drew near the town, the soldier saw a crowd of people pressing out of the town gate, raising loud shouts of joy and waving green branches in the air.
sentences.n: “sich nähern” takes the dative: to draw near to something. “erhuben” is the older past of erheben; modern German has erhoben.

sentences.t: Dann sah er daß die ganze Leibwache herangezogen kam.
sentences.l: Then he saw that the whole bodyguard came marching up.
sentences.i: Then he saw the whole bodyguard coming up.
sentences.n: “herangezogen kam” pairs a participle with kommen — German’s way of saying came doing something.

sentences.t: „Was soll das heißen?“ sprach er ganz verwundert zu dem Jäger.
sentences.l: “What is that supposed to mean?” said he quite astonished to the huntsman.
sentences.i: “What is the meaning of this?” he said to the huntsman, quite astonished.
sentences.n: “heißen” here is to mean, not to be called — the same verb in a second sense a few lines after “hieß”, bade.

sentences.t: „Weißt du nicht“ antwortete er, „daß der König lange Zeit aus seinem Reich entfernt war, heute kehrt er zurück, und da gehen ihm alle entgegen.“
sentences.l: “Do you not know,” answered he, “that the king was away from his kingdom for a long time, today he returns, and so everyone goes out to meet him.”
sentences.i: “Do you not know,” he answered, “that the king has long been away from his kingdom? Today he comes back, and so they are all going out to meet him.”
sentences.n: “entfernt sein von” is to be away from, absent. “entgegen gehen” takes the dative of the person met, here “ihm”.

sentences.t: „Aber wo ist der König“ sprach der Soldat, „ich sehe ihn nicht.“
sentences.l: “But where is the king,” said the soldier, “I do not see him.”
sentences.n: The 1857 printing gives the question no question mark; the speech simply runs on into the speech tag.

sentences.t: „Hier ist er,“ antwortete der Jäger, „ich bin der König und habe meine Ankunft melden lassen.“
sentences.l: “Here he is,” answered the huntsman, “I am the king and have had my arrival announced.”
sentences.i: “Here he is,” answered the huntsman. “I am the king, and I have had my arrival announced.”
sentences.n: “melden lassen” — to have something reported; this is the errand he gave the man at the end of the last scene, and only now does the printing let us see it.

sentences.t: Dann öffnete er seinen Jägerrock, daß man die königlichen Kleider sehen konnte.
sentences.l: Then he opened his huntsman’s coat, so that one could see the royal clothes.
sentences.i: Then he opened his huntsman’s coat, so that the royal clothes could be seen.
sentences.n: The green coat was over the king’s clothes the whole time; the tale has him wear it for eight pages and takes one sentence to undo it.

sentences.t: Der Soldat erschrack, fiel auf die Knie und bat ihn um Vergebung daß er ihn in der Unwissenheit wie seines Gleichen behandelt und ihn mit solchem Namen angeredet habe.
sentences.l: The soldier took fright, fell on his knees and begged him for forgiveness that he had in his ignorance treated him like his own equal and addressed him with such a name.
sentences.i: The soldier was appalled, fell on his knees and begged his forgiveness for having treated him as an equal in his ignorance, and addressed him by such a name.
sentences.n: “seines Gleichen” is a fixed genitive phrase: one of his own kind. “habe … behandelt … angeredet” is the subjunctive of reported speech, which keeps the apology in the soldier’s own words.

sentences.t: Der König aber reichte ihm die Hand und sprach „du bist ein braver Soldat und hast mir das Leben gerettet.
sentences.l: The king however reached him the hand and said “you are a stout soldier and have saved my life.
sentences.i: But the king gave him his hand and said, “you are a stout soldier and you have saved my life.
sentences.n: “brav” of a soldier is worthy and stout-hearted, not well-behaved. The king says plainly what the tale never showed: the soldier’s recklessness in the robbers’ house saved him.

sentences.t: Du sollst keine Noth mehr leiden, ich will schon für dich sorgen.
sentences.l: You shall suffer no want any more, I will provide for you already.
sentences.i: You shall never want again; I will see to you.
sentences.n: “Noth” is the 1857 spelling of Not. “schon” in “ich will schon” is the reassuring particle: never fear, leave it to me.

sentences.t: Und wenn du einmal ein Stück guten Braten essen willst, so gut als in dem Räuberhaus, so komm nur in die königliche Küche.
sentences.l: And if you should ever want to eat a piece of good roast, as good as in the robbers’ house, then just come into the royal kitchen.
sentences.i: And if ever you want a piece of good roast, as good as the one in the robbers’ house, just come to the royal kitchen.
sentences.n: “einmal” here is not “once” but “at some time, ever”. “so gut als” again uses “als” where modern German uses “wie”.

sentences.t: Willst du aber eine Gesundheit ausbringen, so sollst du erst bei mir Erlaubnis dazu holen.“
sentences.l: But if you want to bring out a health, then you shall first fetch permission for it from me.”
sentences.i: But if you want to drink a health, you must first come to me for leave to do it.”
sentences.n: The tale ends on the joke and nothing else: the toast that froze twelve robbers is now a thing the king would rather be asked about first.

glossary.abgehauenen: abhauen — hewn down, felled (past part., inflected; ein abgehauener Baumstamm: a felled tree-trunk)
glossary.alte: die Alte — the old woman (alt ‘old’ substantivized; der Alte: the old man)
glossary.braten: der Braten — roast, joint of meat (masc. noun)
glossary.entfernt: entfernt — away, absent (from entfernen; entfernt sein von: to be far from)
glossary.es: es — it; also the impersonal subject where English needs “there” or a dummy “it” (es wird etwas zu essen geben: there will be something to eat)
glossary.esse: essen — (I) eat (1st sg. present; mit essen: to eat along with them)
glossary.gefallen: gefallen — sich etwas gefallen lassen: to put up with, to allow (infinitive of gefallen, to please)
glossary.gesellt: sich gesellen — joins company (3rd sg. present; gleich und gleich gesellt sich gern: like keeps company with like)
glossary.gesundheit: die Gesundheit — health (eine Gesundheit ausbringen: to drink a health, to propose a toast)
glossary.halten: halten — to hold; of clothing and boots, to last, to hold up (sie halten nicht lange)
glossary.heißen: heißen — to mean, signify (infinitive; was soll das heißen: what is the meaning of this)
glossary.hieß: heißen — bade, ordered (3rd sg. past; jemanden etwas thun heißen: to bid someone do something)
glossary.ihm: ihm — to him, for him; also “to it” for a masculine or neuter noun (dative of er/es)
glossary.kehrt: zurückkehren — returns (3rd sg. present; separable zurück-: kehrt … zurück)
glossary.knallte: knallen — banged, popped (3rd sg. past; of a cork)
glossary.leben: leben — to live (infinitive; ihr sollt alle leben: the ordinary German toast, long life to you all). Also das Leben — life (jemanden ums Leben bringen: to kill)
glossary.macht: machen — makes, does (3rd sg. present; keine Umstände machen: to make no fuss)
glossary.rühren: sich rühren — to stir, to move (infinitive)
glossary.schafft: herbeischaffen — bring here, fetch up (2nd pl. imperative; separable herbei-: schafft … herbei)
glossary.schau: anschauen — look at (imperative sg.; separable an-: schau … an)
glossary.soldaten: der Soldat — soldier (dat./acc. sg., weak noun)
glossary.sorgen: sorgen — to provide, to take care (für jemanden sorgen: to look after someone)
glossary.sperren: aufsperren — open wide (3rd pl. present; separable auf-: sperren … auf; das Maul aufsperren: to gape)
glossary.streckten: strecken — stretched, held out (3rd pl. past)
glossary.stricken: der Strick — ropes, cords (dat. pl.; mit Stricken gebunden: bound with ropes)
glossary.ungestüm: das Ungestüm — impetuosity, vehemence (mit Ungestüm: boisterously)
glossary.weiß: wissen — (I) know (1st sg. present; the spelling is also the adjective weiß, white)
glossary.zog: ziehen — went, drew (3rd sg. past; umher ziehen: to wander about; zog heraus: pulled out, herausziehen)
glossary.zwar: zwar — und zwar: and that specifically, and let it be (introducing a specification)
